what_its_for: Fluconazole is an antifungal medicine used to treat and prevent fungal infections. These include vaginal yeast infections, oral thrush (a yeast infection in your mouth or throat), fungal infections of the esophagus (the tube connecting your mouth to your stomach), urinary tract fungal infections, and certain serious fungal infections that can spread through the body.
how_to_take: Take fluconazole exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food — it does not matter. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. If you are using the liquid form, shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully with the measuring spoon or cup that came with it. Do not use a regular kitchen spoon, as it may not give you the right amount. Take this medicine at the same time each day if you are taking it for more than one dose.
dosing: Your dose will depend on the type of infection being treated and how serious it is. For a vaginal yeast infection, your doctor may prescribe just one single dose (usually 150 mg). For other infections, you may need to take it once a day for several days, weeks, or even months. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose and how long to take it. Do not stop early even if you feel better, unless your doctor tells you to.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this can increase your risk of side effects.
storage: Store fluconazole tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. If you have the liquid suspension, store it at room temperature and throw away any unused portion after 2 weeks. Keep all medications out of the reach of children and pets. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them down the drain unless instructed to do so.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking fluconazole, as it may worsen certain side effects like dizziness or stomach upset. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medications you take, including over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, and herbal supplements, because fluconazole can interact with many medicines. Important interactions include blood thinners like warfarin (Coumadin), certain cholesterol medicines like simvastatin, certain diabetes medicines, certain heart rhythm medicines, and many others. Do not take a new medication without checking with your pharmacist first while on fluconazole.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: a severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling skin; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; difficulty breathing or swallowing; yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); unusual tiredness; dark-colored urine; severe stomach pain or nausea; fast or irregular heartbeat; or seizures. Contact your doctor if your infection does not improve or gets worse, or if you have any side effects that concern you. Common mild side effects like mild nausea, stomach upset, or headache are usually not serious, but tell your doctor if they bother you.
when_it_works: For vaginal yeast infections treated with a single dose, you may start to feel relief within 24 hours, but it can take 2 to 3 days to feel significantly better and up to 7 days for all symptoms to fully go away. For other types of infections that require multiple doses, improvement may take longer — sometimes several days to weeks. Continue taking the medicine for as long as your doctor prescribed, even if your symptoms improve quickly, to make sure the infection is fully cleared.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Fluconazole, especially repeated or high doses, may harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor immediately if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. A single low dose may sometimes be used cautiously, but your doctor will weigh the risks and benefits. Breastfeeding: Fluconazole passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking this medicine. Children: Fluconazole can be used in children, but the dose will be carefully calculated based on the child's weight and type of infection. Older adults and kidney problems: If you are elderly or have kidney disease, your doctor may prescribe a lower dose or have you take it less often, since the drug is removed from the body through the kidneys. Always tell your doctor about all medical conditions you have.
